NewReality.headline: The smarter the world gets, the more your mind is worth.
NewReality.subhead: Everyone's bracing for machines to make them obsolete. They've got it backwards.
NewReality.bodyP1: For the first time, machines can do the things we thought made us smart. They remember everything. They calculate in an instant. They answer before you've finished the question.
NewReality.bodyP2: So what's left? The things they can't do.

NewReality.closing: That last one is the rarest of all. It can't be downloaded. It can't be trained overnight. It's earned, over a lifetime, by a mind that stays sharp.
NewReality.pivot: Which means staying sharp is no longer about holding on. It's about staying ahead. And it starts somewhere smaller than you'd ever think.

Reason.headline: Your brain runs on tiny batteries.
Reason.subhead: Billions of them. And they're the reason you feel sharp — or you don't.
Reason.bodyP1: Your brain is the hungriest part of you. Just 2% of your body, burning 20% of your energy. It never stops, and it never coasts.
Reason.bodyP2: All that energy is made inside your cells by microscopic power plants called mitochondria — your brain's batteries. When they're full and firing, you feel it. Quick. Clear. On.
Reason.bodyP3: But like every battery, they fade with time. Scientists have a name for it: mitochondrial decay. As the batteries weaken, the brain gets less of the one thing it runs on.
Reason.turn: Here's what most people never hear: batteries can be looked after.
Reason.differentiation: Not at the surface. At the source.
Reason.pivot: And we didn't guess at any of this. The roadmap came from thirty years of published research by one neuroscientist.
Reason.calloutLabel: of the body / of its energy

Scientist.headline: Meet Dr. Jiankang Liu.
Scientist.subhead: He has spent thirty years on a single question: how do you keep a brain sharp?
Scientist.bodyP1: In February 2002, three of his papers ran in a single issue of PNAS — the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, one of the most respected journals in science. Most researchers never place a single paper there in a lifetime. He placed three at once.
Scientist.bodyP2: His work has since been cited by other scientists more than 22,000 times.
Scientist.bodyP3: This isn't a wellness trend with a celebrity face. It's a life's work — trained at UC Berkeley, carried through laboratories in the US and abroad, focused on one idea: how the brain makes its energy, and how to help it keep making it.
Scientist.bodyP4: When our founder, Mo Chen, set out to build BiGH, he didn't start with a logo or a launch plan. He started with a scientist he's known for years — and the belief that this research deserved to reach the people who need it.
Scientist.pivot: His research became a formula. We call it NuriCell.
